facts.text: The burrowing owl is a small, long-legged, primarily terrestrial—though not flightless—species of owl native to the open landscapes of North and South America.

facts.text: The great horned owl, also known as the tiger owl or the hoot owl, is a large owl native to the Americas.

facts.text: The red-tailed hawk is a bird of prey and one of the most common hawks in North America.

tagline.text: The hidden ground-seeker of the chaparral, with a borrowed song.

facts.text: The greater yellowlegs is a large shorebird in the family Scolopacidae.
They mainly eat insects and small fish, as well as crustaceans, marine worms, frogs, seeds and berries.
They nest on the ground, usually in well-hidden locations near water.
The call is harsher, louder, and clearer than that of the lesser yellowlegs.
The young leave the nest within 24 hours of hatching and then leave the vicinity of the nest within two days.
Their breeding habitat is bogs and marshes in the boreal forest region of Canada and Alaska.
They migrate to the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of the United States, the Caribbean, and south to South America.
The greater yellowlegs is similar in appearance to the smaller lesser yellowlegs.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 64 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 162 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It lays 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Near Threatened.

sentences.text: Across the bogs and marshes of the northern forest rings a call harsher, louder and clearer than its smaller cousin's.
It belongs to the greater yellowlegs, a large shorebird that nests on the ground, well hidden near water.
Its chicks waste no time: they leave the nest within a day of hatching and soon wander far from it.
Then the bird flies on to the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, the Caribbean, and south to South America.

tagline.text: The loud-voiced shorebird of the northern bogs.

facts.text: The willet is a large shorebird in the family Scolopacidae.
They are territorial both on the breeding grounds and on the wintering areas but form loose breeding colonies or wintering groups.
The male normally leads the female through the territory and creates trial nest scrapes for the female to consider until she selects the site.
The willet's name is onomatopoeic and refers to its loud piercing "pill-will-willet" territorial song., which is higher pitched and repeated at a faster rate in Eastern willets than in Western birds.
The passage of the Migratory Bird Treaty Act in 1918 protected the willet from intensive exploitation by hunters for food and allowed its numbers to rebound to present levels.
When displaying the wings are held stiffly and downcurved in flight while on the ground the display gives prominence to the distinctive pattern of the underwings.
If the nest is placed among grass the female may pull grass stalks over the nest for camouflage.
The eastern willet breeds in coastal saltmarshes while the western willet breeds in freshwater prairie marshes, sloughs, potholes and other inland wetlands.
Its wingspan is about 70 cm.
It weighs about 246 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in coasts.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It lays 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Pill-will-willet rings across the marsh, and so the bird named itself, for "willet" echoes that loud, piercing song.
Eastern birds, bred in coastal saltmarshes, sing it higher and faster than western birds of inland prairie marshes.
The male leads the female through his territory, scratching trial nest scrapes until she picks one.
Among grass, she may pull stalks over the nest to hide it.
A loud voice for the ground it claims, and a hidden home.

tagline.text: It sings its own name across the marsh.

facts.text: The American robin is a migratory bird of the true thrush genus and Turdidae, the wider thrush family.
The species is active mostly during the day and assembles in large flocks at night.
The species is one of the first North American birds to lay eggs, and normally has two to three broods per breeding season, which lasts from April to July.
The male, as with many thrushes, has a complex and almost continuous song.
The Tlingit people of northwestern North America held it to be a culture hero created by Raven to please the people with its song.
Juveniles and eggs are preyed upon by squirrels, snakes, and some birds.
Its diet consists of invertebrates, fruits, and berries.
The flocks break up during the day when the birds feed on fruits and berries in smaller groups.
Its wingspan is about 39 cm.
It weighs about 78 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in forest.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It forages in the air, on the ground and in the trees alike.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 2 to 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: By night the robins gather in great flocks; by day the flocks break apart, and small bands go seeking fruit and berries.
Few North American birds lay eggs sooner, and the robin raises brood after brood from April to July.
And the male sings, his song complex and almost without pause.
The Tlingit people of northwestern North America held that Raven made the robin to please the people with that song.

tagline.text: The thrush that Raven made to sing.

facts.text: The western kingbird is a large tyrant flycatcher found throughout western North America, as far south as Mexico.
Kingbirds make a sturdy cup nest in a tree or shrub, sometimes on top of a pole or other man-made structure.
Vocalizations from this species often consist of a long series of squeaky bubbling calls, sometimes compared to a squeaky toy.
Adults are a combination of both gray and yellow plumage, along with crimson feathers that are hidden until courtship or against intruders.
Three to five white, creamy, or pinkish eggs with heavy blotches of brown, black, or lavender are laid and incubated for 12 to 14 days.
Characteristic of kingbird species, the western kingbird is very territorial.
The breeding habitat is open areas in western North America.
Instances of hybridization with the closely related Eastern Kingbird have been reported.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 37 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 40 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in shrubland.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 2 to 7 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Across the open lands of western North America, the western kingbird keeps watch from tree and shrub.
Like all kingbirds, it guards its ground fiercely.
Its voice is no trumpet, just a long run of squeaky, bubbling calls, like a toy.
But this gray-and-yellow king hides a secret: crimson feathers, shown only in courtship or against intruders.
Its throne is a sturdy cup nest, sometimes set atop a pole.

tagline.text: The squeaky-voiced king who keeps its crimson hidden.

facts.text: The barn owl is recognized by most taxonomic authorities.
Like most owls, it is nocturnal, relying on its acute sense of hearing when hunting in complete darkness.
Barn owls living in tropical regions can breed at any time of year, but some seasonality in nesting is still evident.
Intensification of agricultural practices often means that the rough grassland that provides the best foraging habitat is lost.
Nestlings are covered in white down, but the heart-shaped facial disk becomes visible soon after hatching.
It often becomes active shortly before dusk and can sometimes be seen during the day when relocating from one roosting site to another.
Where there are distinct wet and dry seasons, egg-laying usually takes place during the dry season, with increased rodent prey becoming available to the birds as the vegetation dies off.
An insufficiency of suitable nesting sites may be another factor limiting barn owl numbers.
Its wingspan is about 98 cm.
It weighs about 403 g.
It feeds mostly on other vertebrates.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a cavity or a crevice.
It lays 1 to 7 eggs in a clutch.

sentences.text: Shortly before dusk the barn owl stirs, and is sometimes seen by day, moving between roosts.
In complete darkness it hunts by its keen hearing.
Where wet and dry seasons turn, it lays in the dry time, as plants die back and rodents grow plenty.
Its chicks hatch in white down, the heart-shaped face showing soon after.
But heavy farming eats the rough grassland where it hunts best, and too few nest sites can mean fewer owls.

tagline.text: Heart-faced hunter that listens through the dark.

facts.text: The warbling vireo is a small North American songbird.
It often nests in widely spaced trees, often cottonwood or aspen, along streams or rivers.
Warbling vireos forage for insects in trees, hopping along branches and sometimes hovering.
They make a deep cup nest suspended from a tree branch or shrub, placed relatively high in the east and lower in the west.
The male helps with incubation and may sing from the nest.
The song is a cheerful warble, similar to that of the painted bunting and the purple finch.
Its breeding habitat is open deciduous and mixed woods from Alaska to Mexico.
It migrates to Mexico and Central America.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 22 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 13 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in forest.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 1 to 5 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Where cottonwood and aspen stand wide apart along a river, the warbling vireo keeps house.
It hangs a deep cup nest from a branch, high in the east and lower in the west.
Then comes its small wonder: the male takes his turn on the eggs, and he may sing right from the nest.
His song is a cheerful warble, much like the songs of the painted bunting and the purple finch.

tagline.text: The father who sings from the nest.

facts.text: The yellow-headed blackbird is a medium-sized blackbird with a yellow head.
They forage in marshes, fields, or on the ground, sometimes catching insects in flight.
The nest is built with and attached to marsh vegetation and is constructed over open water.
Male yellow-headed blackbirds have been observed to have two types of songs, an "accent song" and a "buzz song".
Yellow‐headed blackbirds have been found to be sensitive to nest predation risk, for example by marsh wrens, and alter their nest attendance behavior accordingly.
Sunflowers are fairly popular amongst yellow-headed blackbirds in the Northern Great Plains, with a study indicating that males eat more sunflower than grains and females more grains than sunflower.
They nest in colonies, often sharing their habitat closely with the red-winged blackbird.
The "buzz songs'' have much higher pitch than the accent song, and thus do not echo as well in the dense marshes they live in.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 38 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 63 g.
It feeds mostly on seeds.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
Some of its populations migrate and others stay all year.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 2 to 5 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Over open water, it builds its nest from marsh plants and fastens it among them.
It nests in colonies, its neighbors close, often beside the red-winged blackbird.
It minds the danger of nest robbers such as the marsh wren, and changes how it tends its nest.
The male sings two songs, an accent song and a buzz song.
The buzz is pitched much higher, so it echoes less well through the thick marsh.

tagline.text: A golden head above a nest built over open water.

facts.text: The white-winged dove is a dove whose native range extends from the Southwestern United States through Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean.
The call is likened to the English phrase "who cooks for you".
Normally, up to 4000 birds are seen migrating, but in Texas, a flock of up to a million birds was recorded.
Males may aggressively defend territory from other males, sparring with wing slaps.
White-winged doves are popular as game birds for hunting.
In recent years with increasing urbanization and backyard feeding, it has expanded throughout Texas, into Oklahoma, Louisiana, and coastal Mississippi.
White-winged doves are subjected to the usual arid-land predators, including foxes, bobcats, snakes, and coyotes.
Their diet consists mostly of grains, but will also include pollen and nectar, especially from the saguaro cactus, which is a vital source of water.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 49 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 153 g.
It feeds mostly on seeds.
It lives mostly in shrubland.
It stays in its range all year.
It forages in the air, on the ground and in the trees alike.
It nests in a platform.
It lays 2 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Out where the saguaro stands, this bird sips the cactus's pollen and nectar, a vital source of water.
Mostly, though, it eats grains.
Its call, folks say, sounds like a question: who cooks for you?
Males may fiercely guard their ground from other males, sparring with slaps of the wing.
And as towns grew and backyards set out food, it spread across Texas and on into Oklahoma, Louisiana and coastal Mississippi.

tagline.text: It sips from the cactus and calls, who cooks for you?

facts.text: The mourning dove is a member of the dove family, Columbidae.
Mourning doves eat almost exclusively seeds, but the young are fed crop milk by their parents.
Outside the breeding season, mourning doves roost communally in dense deciduous trees or conifers.
Courtship begins with a noisy flight by the male, followed by a graceful, circular glide with outstretched wings and head down.
During the call, the throat of the dove swells.
The "mourning" part of its common name comes from its doleful call.
Migration is usually during the day, in flocks, and at low altitudes.
As a gamebird, the mourning dove is well-managed, with more than 20 million shot by hunters each year.
Its wingspan is about 43 cm.
It weighs about 119 g.
It feeds mostly on seeds.
It lives mostly in towns, farms and other places people have changed.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It lays 2 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: The mourning dove wears its name for its call, a doleful song.
As it sings, its throat swells round with the sound.
To win a mate, the male bursts up in a noisy flight, then glides in a graceful circle, wings stretched wide and head bowed down.
Seeds are nearly all it eats, yet its young are fed crop milk by their parents.
When the breeding season ends, the doves gather to roost together in dense trees.

tagline.text: A sorrowful song, a swelling throat, a graceful circling glide.

facts.text: The white-crowned sparrow is a species of passerine bird native to North America.
They mainly eat seeds, other plant parts and insects.
In winter, they often forage in flocks.
It breeds in brushy areas in the taiga and tundra of the northernmost parts of the continent and in the Rocky Mountains and Pacific coast.
The scientific name is from Ancient Greek.
Their breeding habitat is brushy areas across northern Canada and the western United States.
Adults have black and white stripes on their head, a gray face, brown streaked upper parts and a long tail.
A medium-sized member of the New World sparrow family, this species is marked by a grey face and black and white streaking on the upper head.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 24 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 28 g.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in shrubland.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It forages in the air, on the ground and in the trees alike.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 3 to 7 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: A crown of black and white stripes marks the white-crowned sparrow, set above a gray face.
It breeds in brushy places on the northern taiga and tundra, in the Rocky Mountains and along the Pacific coast.
There it nests in a cup.
In winter the crowned ones gather in flocks to forage.
Seeds, other plant parts and insects are their fare, found on the ground, in the trees, even in the air.

tagline.text: A striped crown, from tundra brush to winter flocks.
